newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU says U.S. jeopardising computer tariffs deal.
newsitem.headline: EU says U.S. jeopardising computer tariffs deal.

text.p: The European Commission accused the United States on Thursday of jeopardising a global pact on ending tariffs on computer-related goods by pushing for delays and exemptions.

"Some of us are beginning to reach the conclusion the United States is not seriously interested in reaching an agreement in Singapore," a Commission official told reporters, referring to a World Trade Organisation ministerial meeting next month.

The official, in comments timed to coincide with a meeting of Asia-Pacific countries in Manila, said the European Union could not accept the U.S. effort to exclude four major products from the proposed Information Technology Agreement (ITA).

"Any request by a participant to exempt products from coverage can only invite others to do the same," European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said in statement IP/96/1064 aimed at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.
"The major industrialised countries, including in particular Japan and the U.S. as well as the (EU), have to set an example for others to follow."
The official derided what he called the "topsy turvy" situation where the United States, rather than Asian countries, seemed to pose the greatest threat to the pact.
U.S. government and industry officials dismissed the charges, saying Washington had led the ITA effort and that agreeing on product coverage was a normal part of negotiations.
"You could say we initiated this negotiation and we're pushing it harder than anybody," a U.S. official told Reuters.
"Our entire negotiating team is in Manila right now at the APEC summit to encourage the most extensive Asian participation possible."
The ITA would eliminate duties on a range of electronic products, including computers, software, semiconductors and telecommunications equipment.

The Commission official, who asked not to be named, said the United States had succumbed to industry lobbying and proposed excluding four important product categories -- capacitors, fibre-optic cables, graphic monitors and photocopiers.
He said the EU and the United States also differed over the timescale for the cuts, with the EU favouring a 1999 deadline and Washington proposing 2000.

Greg Garcia, director of international trade affairs for the American Electronics Association in Washington, said the United States had proposed ending tariffs on an extensive list of several hundred products and had agreed to exclude the consumer electronics industry at Europe's request.

"My view is that these are the noises you hear in the closing days of trade negotiations when you pick out a few issues and blow them out of proportion to see what else you can extract from your negotiating partners."
The Commission official said the EU was encouraged by the positive response to the ITA initiative by Asian countries including South Korea, the Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia.
The U.S. official agreed that Asian countries were proving receptive and expressed optimism about the ITA talks. "The negotiation is at an intensive phase and proceeding reasonably well," he said.
